pitfalls: Advice given verbally pitch-side is easily forgotten without a take-home card → make the printed card, not verbal advice alone, the pass criterion
Volunteers may not have the card to hand on the day → check kit stock as part of the pre-season safety check
Under-18s need advice given to both player and parent/carer → record this separately from adult cases
Cards go out of date if guidance is updated → check the card version matches the current national guidance at each audit
pearls: Download the free UK Concussion Guidelines information card rather than designing a new one
Combine information-card distribution with the removal-from-play form so both happen at the same pitch-side moment
Ask parents/carers directly (brief survey) whether they received and understood the advice
Refresh first-aid kit stock checks at the start of each new season, not only when an incident occurs

pitfalls: Contact details for parents/carers may be out of date → verify emergency contact details at the start of each season
Away fixtures make same-day face-to-face contact harder → accept a documented phone call as equivalent
Coaches may assume another adult (a relative at the match) has informed the parent → make the coach personally responsible for confirming this
Player embarrassment may lead to under-reporting to parents → frame the policy as standard practice for every knock, not a special report
pearls: Build parental contact into the same incident form used for the removal-from-play audit
Brief parents at the start of the season on what to expect if their child is suspected of a concussion
Use the club's existing safeguarding lead, who already holds emergency contact responsibilities
Share a simple parent-facing information sheet alongside the player-facing concussion card

pitfalls: Staff move between departments or trusts before the check is due → flag the pending check in a shared occupational health system rather than a single department log
Blood test uptake among busy staff is often poor → offer testing at the workplace or during an existing appointment
Non-responder status is not always acted on → link this audit to a booster/re-testing pathway for non-responders
New starters may complete the course at a previous employer → confirm completion dates carefully before including a case
pearls: Use the occupational health vaccination database's own recall function rather than a manual spreadsheet
Offer drop-in phlebotomy sessions timed to when most staff are due their check
Report responder/non-responder rates separately, since non-responders need a distinct pathway
Recruit the occupational health nurse manager as audit lead, since they already run the vaccination programme

pitfalls: Non-responders may be a small, scattered group → collect over 2 years to reach a meaningful sample
Staff may not attend for a repeat course once already vaccinated → explain the individual risk of remaining a non-responder clearly
Some non-responders are never confirmed as HBsAg-negative → include this as an acceptable alternative management outcome
Occupational health records may be split across paper and electronic systems → check both sources before concluding a plan is missing
pearls: Base the pathway design on the Green Book's own guidance on further doses and testing
Recruit the occupational health physician for clinical sign-off of the pathway
Track outcomes long-term (does a repeat course convert non-responders?) as a natural extension of this audit
Share anonymised non-responder numbers with the trust's infection prevention team, who share an interest in exposure risk

pitfalls: Out-of-hours exposures are the highest-risk group for delay, since occupational health is usually closed → ensure the ED pathway covers all hours
HBIG needs a same-day source patient hepatitis B test where status is unknown → build rapid testing into the pathway
Small numbers of eligible exposures → extend the sampling period to the last 2–3 years
Staff may delay reporting an injury out of embarrassment or workload pressure → reinforce a no-blame reporting culture
pearls: Base the local pathway directly on the Green Book's own post-exposure timing wording
Agree HBIG stock-holding and rapid access with pharmacy and the ED lead before cycle 1
Recruit the infection control team, who already investigate needlestick incidents, as co-auditors
Track time-to-first-vaccine-dose as a secondary measure, since this drives the 24-hour HBIG window

pitfalls: Incident reporting systems capture what happened but not always when advice was first sought → cross-check with occupational health call logs
Staff may assume a low-risk source means advice is unnecessary → make advice-seeking mandatory regardless of perceived risk
Night-shift staff may not know who to call → ensure the out-of-hours contact is on the card, not only daytime numbers
Under-reporting remains a barrier even with cards in place → reinforce reporting culture alongside the practical change
pearls: Involve ward and theatre staff in designing the card so the wording is clear and short
Place cards exactly where sharps injuries happen (sinks, sharps bins), not only in notice boards
Use the same incident case list as the HBIG-timing audit to cover the whole needlestick pathway in one data collection round
Report near-miss data (advice sought quickly even without HBIG) as a positive indicator alongside the compliance rate

pitfalls: Agency and bank staff may bypass the trust's own pre-employment process → check the pathway covers all staff groups, not only substantive posts
Assessments completed but the immunisation section left blank → treat a blank section as a fail, not an assumed pass
Starting before the assessment is complete under service pressure → agree an escalation process for urgent starts with HR
COSHH risk assessment by role (which pathogens staff are exposed to) needs to inform which immunisations are offered → check this link is made, not assumed
pearls: Use the Green Book's own COSHH risk-assessment framework to structure which immunisations are checked by role
Recruit HR/recruitment alongside occupational health, since start dates are set jointly
Present a simple 'before and after' comparison of the questionnaire form to show the change clearly
Track time from job offer to completed assessment as a secondary measure to catch late starts

pitfalls: Bank, agency and night staff are often missed by daytime campaigns → schedule peer vaccinator visits across all shifts
Staff who move between departments during the season may be double-counted or missed → use a single trust-wide tracker, not ward-level lists alone
Declining staff should have this recorded, not left blank → treat a blank record as 'not offered', not 'declined'
Campaign timing (early in the season) affects the denominator if staff join partway through → clarify the eligible cohort before cycle 1
pearls: Use the trust's existing flu campaign peer vaccinator network as the audit's data collectors
Present ward-by-ward offer rates to identify areas needing extra visits
Report offer rate and uptake rate separately, since this audit is about the offer being made, not just uptake
Time the audit to coincide with the mid-campaign review point so results can still influence that season's efforts

pitfalls: Patients under shared care between GP and mental health services can fall between the two → agree who owns the recall before cycle 1
Patients who avoid blood tests are hardest to reach → offer a point-of-care or home phlebotomy option where available
A hard stop on prescribing needs pharmacy system changes → involve pharmacy IT from the outset
Register accuracy depends on all lithium patients being correctly coded → check the register against a full drug search before starting
pearls: Base the recall directly on the original NPSA alert's own 3-month standard so the audit maps onto a nationally recognised benchmark
Use the NPSA lithium record book (patient-held) as a low-cost extra safety net alongside the electronic recall
Recruit a mental health pharmacist to lead, since they typically run the lithium register already
Report separately for primary and secondary care patients, since the fix may differ by setting

pitfalls: Renal and thyroid tests are sometimes requested separately from the lithium level, causing extra venepuncture visits → combine them on one request form
Deteriorating renal function may not trigger a dose review → link abnormal results to a documented lithium dose review action
Test results filed but not reviewed by a prescriber → require a clinician sign-off field, not just a filed result
Register may not distinguish patients newly started from established patients → exclude the first 6 months, which has its own more frequent monitoring schedule
pearls: Combine data collection with the lithium level audit above, since both use the same register and time period
Ask the laboratory to bundle lithium, renal and thyroid tests under a single 'lithium monitoring panel' order code
Recruit the same mental health pharmacist leading the lithium level audit
Track abnormal results and the action taken as a secondary measure of monitoring quality, not just test completion

pitfalls: Booklets and alert cards can run out of stock → assign restocking responsibility to a named pharmacist
Patients started as inpatients may be discharged before receiving the pack → check discharge as well as initiation records
Record books can be lost by the patient over time → check for a record book at each subsequent review, not just at initiation
Digital patient-held records are increasingly used instead of paper → accept an equivalent digital record as a pass
pearls: Order NPSA-format record books/alert cards in bulk so they are always available at initiation
Give the pharmacist dispensing the first lithium prescription responsibility for checking the pack is complete
Ask patients at their first follow-up review whether they still have their record book, as a simple ongoing check
Present this audit alongside the monitoring-frequency audits for a complete picture of the lithium safety pathway

pitfalls: Ingestion time is often uncertain even in 'single acute' presentations → verify with ambulance or collateral history where possible
Laboratory turnaround for the paracetamol level can itself delay treatment → consider point-of-care testing if turnaround exceeds 1 hour
Patients presenting very close to 8 hours may be missed if the level result is delayed → treat empirically if delay risks missing the window, per local policy
Excluding staggered overdoses accurately requires a clear definition agreed with data collectors before cycle 1
pearls: Agree with the laboratory a rapid turnaround target for paracetamol levels, since this is often the rate-limiting step
Use the same case-finding method (toxicology coding) as the existing staggered-overdose audit to build a complete paracetamol overdose picture
Recruit the ED pharmacist to review flagged cases in real time during cycle 1
Present findings alongside the NPIS/TOXBASE contact audit below, since both use the same case list

pitfalls: Staff may check TOXBASE but not record having done so → require the reference number, not just a tick-box, as evidence
TOXBASE guidance changes periodically → confirm which version was current at the time of each case if discrepancies arise
Complex or unusual cases may need a telephone call in addition to TOXBASE → capture both contact methods separately
Locum or agency ED staff may be unfamiliar with local access arrangements → include TOXBASE access in induction
pearls: Combine this audit with the acetylcysteine-timing audit above, using the same case list
Display the TOXBASE login and NPIS phone number prominently at every ED workstation
Recruit the ED toxicology or pharmacy lead as audit champion
Use real anonymised cases from cycle 1 as teaching examples for induction of new ED staff

pitfalls: Monitored dosage systems (dosette boxes) are a recognised exception → record these separately, not as non-compliance
Pack sizes may not match the prescribed quantity exactly, tempting repackaging → stock a range of licensed pack sizes to reduce this pressure
Patient cards can run out at the pharmacy → check stock as part of the audit
Dispensing software may not have a field for this at all → this audit's main output may be the business case for adding one
pearls: Use this audit to build the business case for a dispensing-system hard stop, even if the first cycle result is poor
Recruit the chief pharmacist and a community pharmacy contractor (if auditing primary care dispensing) as co-leads
Reference the specific MHRA safety update number when briefing dispensing staff, so the requirement is clearly not just local policy
Check patient card stock alongside pack compliance, since one often reveals the other

pitfalls: General radiology waiting lists can push epilepsy MRIs beyond 6 weeks → a ring-fenced slot needs radiology capacity agreement, not just a policy statement
Regionally agreed epilepsy MRI protocols may not be locally documented → confirm the protocol exists and is used before starting
Excluded epilepsy syndromes (idiopathic generalised, self-limited with centrotemporal spikes) must be correctly identified to avoid skewing the denominator
Children may need a general anaesthetic for MRI, adding delay → record this as a distinct, expected cause of delay
pearls: Agree the ring-fenced slot numbers with radiology using cycle 1 referral volume data
Recruit the epilepsy specialist nurse to track referrals and flag approaching deadlines
Use the same case list as the first-seizure clinic audit to build a complete diagnostic pathway picture
Report scan-to-diagnosis-confirmed time as a secondary measure of overall pathway speed

pitfalls: Discussion may happen verbally but not be recorded in the letter → require the field to be in the templated letter, not left to free text
Patients below driving age at diagnosis still need future advice → record this as 'deferred, to be discussed before driving age' rather than a straightforward fail
Letters dictated and typed later may lag behind the consultation, delaying documentation → use a same-day templated letter where possible
DVLA rules change periodically → check the letter template references current DVLA guidance at each audit
pearls: Build the driving field into the same templated letter build as the care-plan-copy audit below, so both changes happen together
Provide clinicians with a one-line DVLA notification prompt card to use during the consultation
Recruit the epilepsy specialist nurse, who often reiterates this discussion at follow-up
Share DVLA's own patient information leaflet at the same appointment to reinforce the discussion

pitfalls: Letters typed and posted after the appointment may never explicitly confirm a copy reached the patient → track 'given at appointment' separately from 'posted later'
Care plans for children may need a version appropriate for the child as well as the parent → check both were considered
Clinic time pressure can make same-visit printing impractical → agree realistic clinic template time with the service before cycle 1
Patients who prefer a digital copy should still be offered one, recorded as an equivalent pass
pearls: Combine this audit's data collection with the driving-discussion audit, since both use the same clinic letters
Ask reception or clinic support staff to print and hand over the plan at check-out, taking pressure off clinicians
Offer an electronic copy via the patient portal as an alternative to a paper copy
Use patient feedback (a short survey) to confirm plans given were actually understood, not just handed over

pitfalls: This applies to all anti-seizure medications, not only valproate, so existing valproate-specific systems will not fully capture it → build a medication-agnostic field
Young girls not yet needing contraception discussions may still need age-appropriate risk information → include this group explicitly, not just adult women
Discussions at GP-led reviews (rather than specialist clinic) may be missed if only specialist letters are checked → clarify which setting is in scope before cycle 1
Patients seen only by telephone may have shorter, less complete documentation → check both face-to-face and telephone clinic letters
pearls: Use the same clinic caseload list as any existing valproate ARAF audit to avoid duplicating case-finding work
Recruit the epilepsy specialist nurse, who often leads these discussions in practice
Provide clinicians with a short structured prompt card covering all anti-seizure medications with teratogenic risk, not only valproate
Report findings by medication class to show where risk communication is strongest and weakest

pitfalls: This standard covers four specific drugs, not all anti-seizure medications, so the alert must be drug-specific to avoid unnecessary prompts
Contraception method may be managed entirely in primary care and not visible to the neurology clinic → check both GP and specialist records
Non-hormonal or copper IUD users need this explicitly recorded as 'not applicable' rather than being marked as a fail
Topiramate's own separate Pregnancy Prevention Programme requirements (already audited) may overlap with this general interaction advice → keep the pass criteria distinct
pearls: Coordinate with the existing topiramate Pregnancy Prevention Programme audit to avoid double data collection on the same patients
Provide a simple interaction quick-reference card (drug name, effect on contraception, alternative advice) for clinicians
Recruit a contraception/sexual health lead as an occasional co-reviewer for complex cases
Report by individual drug, since carbamazepine, phenytoin, oxcarbazepine and topiramate caseloads may differ in size

pitfalls: ED coding may not clearly distinguish a seizure-related attendance from other reasons → cross-check with the triage complaint as well as the diagnosis code
Epilepsy specialist nurse capacity may not match ED attendance volume → agree a realistic response model (call-back, not always a face-to-face session) with the service before cycle 1
Attendances out of hours or at weekends may be harder to flag for follow-up → build the referral into the discharge process itself, not a manual daily list
Patients who decline contact should be recorded as offered but declined, not as non-compliance
pearls: Base the automatic referral trigger on the same seizure-related attendance coding used for existing seizure audits
Recruit the epilepsy specialist nurse team directly, since they are best placed to say what response is realistic
Track whether ED re-attendance rates change over time as a secondary outcome of better specialist nurse contact
Present this alongside the referral-to-first-seizure-clinic audit for a fuller picture of the epilepsy urgent care pathway

pitfalls: Sample drawn but result not checked out of hours → build the check into the nursing handover, not just the request
Small numbers at units doing few parathyroidectomies → combine thyroid and parathyroid cases for the denominator
Definition of 'checked' drifts between cycles (requested vs resulted) → fix the definition as 'result available in EPR' before cycle 1
New starters unaware of the algorithm → laminate the algorithm in recovery and on the ward
pearls: Recruit the endocrine surgery clinical nurse specialist to check for missed 12-hour bloods each morning
Agree the exact cut-off time (12h from skin closure, not from admission) before cycle 1 starts
Link the order set to the procedure code so it fires automatically
Keep the same nurse-led calcium round after the surgical trainees rotate

pitfalls: No ENT or voice clinic slots available → negotiate a ring-fenced weekly slot before cycle 1
Refusals not distinguished from omissions → add a separate 'declined' field so the denominator is fair
Surgeons doing their own transcutaneous ultrasound assessment not counted → agree what counts as 'laryngoscopy' before starting
Result not filed back into the surgical record → ask ENT to copy the surgical team into every report
pearls: Agree with ENT a same-day or next-day slot before starting the first cycle
Use a transcutaneous laryngeal ultrasound pathway where trained staff exist, to reduce reliance on ENT capacity
Put the laryngoscopy step on the WHO-style discharge checklist so it cannot be missed
Feed back cord palsy rates to the department each year so the mandatory step is not seen as a paperwork exercise

pitfalls: Voice change not systematically asked about at clinic → add a standard voice question to the pre-assessment template
Small numbers if malignancy is rare locally → run over 6 months rather than 3
Laryngoscopy done but not documented in the surgical notes → require the ENT report to be filed in the same record
MDT proforma completed retrospectively → complete it in real time at the MDT
pearls: Add the voice question to every thyroid nodule clinic template, not just cancer clinics
Use the MDT coordinator to check the field is complete before the case is listed
Share abnormal pre-op findings with the operating surgeon before consent
Keep a log of pre-op abnormal cords to compare with post-op findings

pitfalls: Structural persistence identified in a non-cancer clinic and not flagged → educate all clinicians reviewing thyroid cancer follow-up scans
MDT list overloaded, cases delayed → create a fast-track 'persistent disease' slot
Ambiguity over what counts as 'structural' vs biochemical → agree the definition with radiology and oncology before cycle 1
Retrospective identification bias if reliant on memory → use a coded database search
pearls: Ask radiology to use a standard phrase ('structural persistent disease') in reports to enable searching
Give the MDT coordinator a standing search of the radiology system each week
Keep a register of persistent disease cases for continuity when staff rotate
Feed outcomes back to the referring endocrinologist so follow-up plans are updated

pitfalls: ROSE requires a cytotechnologist or pathologist present at every list → negotiate cover before starting the change
Operator-level data seen as punitive → present anonymised operator codes first, agree feedback approach with the team
Thy1c cases wrongly counted as inadequate → use the coded cytology categories, not free text
Small numbers per individual operator → report at service level first, individual level only with consent
pearls: Agree with cytology in advance which category counts as 'inadequate' for the audit
Use a dedicated ultrasound-guided FNAC list run by trained operators to improve consistency
Share Thy1 rates quarterly at the endocrine surgery/radiology joint meeting
Track repeat-biopsy rate as a secondary outcome

pitfalls: Patients lost to follow-up after discharge from surgical clinic → use a single named follow-up pathway owner
Ultrasound slots not protected for surveillance → agree a standing allocation with radiology
Definition of T1a(m) vs T1a ambiguous to non-specialists → confirm staging with the MDT coordinator for each case
Surveillance stopped early without documented reason → require a reason field if follow-up is curtailed before 5 years
pearls: Use the MDT outcome form to auto-generate the follow-up schedule
Give patients a printed follow-up plan at their post-op clinic visit
Audit alongside the cancer MDT's annual outcomes review
Nominate a CNS to track the pathway centrally

pitfalls: Digoxin still used from habit → remove it as an option from the order set
Bradycardia or hypotension used as a blanket reason to omit prophylaxis without considering alternatives → require the alternative agent to be considered first
AF occurring after ICU discharge missed by the audit → extend data collection to hospital discharge
Anaesthetists and surgeons prescribing inconsistently → agree a single default order set for both teams
pearls: Build the three options into a single tick-box so an active choice is required
Involve pharmacy in checking interactions before amiodarone loading
Review the order set uptake weekly during the first cycle
Keep the postoperative AF rate as a linked outcome measure

pitfalls: Patients discharged to GP follow-up only, with no cardiology review booked → give GPs a clear stop/review date on the discharge letter
Reassessment done but not documented in a retrievable place → use a coded discharge summary field
Loss to follow-up if patients move between services → name a single team responsible for the review
Antiarrhythmics continued indefinitely 'to be safe' → present the evidence for time-limited use at teaching sessions
pearls: Give a clear stop/review date on every antiarrhythmic prescription at discharge
Use the cardiac surgery nurse specialist to track outstanding reviews
Feed reassessment outcomes back to the prescribing team
Align the review with an existing 6-week post-cardiac-surgery follow-up appointment where possible

pitfalls: Statin omitted because the patient is nil by mouth and not represented once feeding resumes → add a re-check step once oral intake restarts
Reconciliation done by a junior doctor without pharmacy cross-check → involve pharmacy in every post-op reconciliation
Statin stopped for a genuine reason (e.g. rhabdomyolysis risk) but not documented → require a reason field
Discharge summary omits the statin even though it was continued in hospital → check the discharge letter as well as the inpatient chart
pearls: Use the electronic medicines reconciliation list as the single source of truth for pre-op medicines
Ask pharmacy to review post-cardiac-surgery drug charts within 24 hours
Flag any statin omission for consultant sign-off
Repeat the check at discharge as well as on the ward

pitfalls: Mechanical prophylaxis omitted because of leg swelling or drains → give clear guidance on device choice around chest drains and vein harvest sites
LMWH delayed because of concern about bleeding after cardiopulmonary bypass → agree a standard start day with the surgical team before cycle 1
7-day course not completed because of early discharge → include a discharge prescription for the remaining days
VTE risk assessment completed but not linked to a prescribing action → link the assessment directly to the order set
pearls: Build both mechanical and pharmacological prophylaxis into a single order-set bundle
Agree the LMWH start time with cardiac surgery and anaesthesia in advance
Audit alongside existing VTE risk-assessment compliance data
Keep a discharge checklist item for completing the 7-day course

pitfalls: 'Decision made' not consistently documented, making the start point unclear → agree a single documentation point (referral form date) before cycle 1
Procedure delayed by lack of ultrasound-trained operators → identify capacity gaps early
Urgent cases wrongly counted against the 5-day target → add an explicit urgent-indication field
Referrals lost between teams → use a single electronic referral pathway
pearls: Use a single electronic referral form that timestamps the decision
Protect a weekly list specifically for non-urgent pleural procedures
Involve the pleural nurse specialist in tracking waiting referrals
Review the waiting list weekly at the pleural MDT

pitfalls: Advice given verbally but not documented → make documentation itself, not just the conversation, the pass criterion
Leaflet given but generic (not sternal-wound specific) → develop a cardiac-surgery-specific leaflet
Patients discharged out of hours without the usual checklist → audit weekend/evening discharges separately
Field ticked as a default without the conversation happening → spot-check with post-discharge phone calls
pearls: Make the leaflet part of the standard cardiac surgery discharge pack
Give the same information to family/carers where the patient has reduced capacity
Include the sternal wound infection bundle as an agenda item at governance meetings
Track re-presentation rates for wound infection as a linked outcome

pitfalls: Decision-to-operate time not documented consistently → agree a single trigger point (consultant/registrar decision documented in notes) before cycle 1
Theatre unavailable out of hours → confirm the emergency theatre escalation pathway covers torsion explicitly
Low case numbers per quarter → collect over 12 months to get a meaningful sample
Fasting status used to justify delay despite clinical urgency → reiterate that assessment should not be delayed by fasting status
pearls: Agree the torsion pathway with emergency medicine, theatres and anaesthesia before starting
Use a single-page torsion pathway sheet that timestamps each step
Review every case with a time over 3 hours at the morbidity and mortality meeting
Track testicular salvage rate as the outcome that matters to families

pitfalls: Transfer driven by lack of confidence rather than genuine need → provide simulation training for on-call teams
Reasons for transfer not documented → make a reason field mandatory in the transfer request
Network guidance not known to on-call staff → include the pathway in induction
Transfer perceived as 'safer' despite adding delay → present time-to-theatre and salvage outcome data alongside transfer rates
pearls: Use network-level data sharing so all sites can benchmark
Keep an up-to-date on-call competency list for out-of-hours cover
Debrief every transferred case at the regional network meeting
Track testicular salvage rate for transferred versus locally-managed cases

pitfalls: Parental expectation of surgery at first visit → provide written information explaining the conservative-first approach
GP referrals arriving without a trial of conservative management → use the proforma to triage these back with advice
Diagnosis of 'physiological' vs 'pathological' inconsistent between clinicians → agree diagnostic criteria before cycle 1
Steroid trial started but not followed up to assess response → build in a documented review
pearls: Give GPs a simple traffic-light referral form so conservative options are tried first
Use a patient information leaflet to manage parental expectations before the clinic visit
Audit alongside circumcision rates for physiological phimosis as an outcome measure
Keep the pathway visible in the electronic referral system

pitfalls: Steroid prescribed by GP but response not fed back to secondary care → ask GPs to document response on the referral back to clinic
Trial too short to assess benefit → specify the recommended 4-week minimum course in the template
Steroid cream not available or not prescribed correctly (wrong strength) → provide a standard prescription card
Circumcision listed 'just in case' before the steroid trial completes → make the field a hard stop on the listing form
pearls: Give parents written instructions on how to apply the steroid and for how long
Ask the GP to review response after 4 weeks rather than waiting for the next hospital appointment
Track circumcision avoidance rate as a secondary outcome
Review any listing without a documented trial at the departmental meeting

pitfalls: List order changes on the day, leaving children over-fasted despite correct initial instructions → actively offer fluids to children further down the list
Ward staff defaulting to traditional 'nil by mouth from midnight' habits → retrain ward and pre-admission staff
Parents fasting children for longer than instructed out of caution → explain the rationale clearly in pre-admission information
Fluid type not actually 'clear' (e.g. milk given) → define clear fluids explicitly in patient information
pearls: Actively offer clear fluids on the ward rather than relying on parents to remember
Update pre-admission letters and phone calls to state the 1-hour rule clearly
Reorder theatre lists to minimise fasting time for younger children
Audit fasting times alongside cancellation rates for over-fasted children

pitfalls: Breastfeeding mothers given the same 6-hour instruction as formula feeders → make the distinction explicit in written information
List order changes causing unplanned prolonged fasting → build a fallback offer of a snack/feed if delay is expected
Fasting times recorded inconsistently (last 'meal' vs last 'snack') → define clearly what counts as a solid feed
Ward staff unaware of the different breast milk time → include in induction training
pearls: Print the age-specific fasting table on ward information boards
Give parents a written personalised fasting time on the day-before phone call
Prioritise younger children and breastfed infants earlier on the list
Review any case with fasting over 8 hours as an outlier

pitfalls: Home blood pressure readings not considered when clinic readings are borderline → offer home/ambulatory monitoring where available
Proteinuria result out of date, leading to the wrong target being applied → require an annual protein:creatinine ratio
Single reading used rather than an average → standardise to the documented clinic reading process
Target-focused prescribing without checking calcineurin inhibitor levels → review nephrotoxic drug levels alongside blood pressure
pearls: Display the applicable target automatically in the clinic template based on the latest proteinuria result
Offer home blood pressure monitoring kits to patients with white-coat effect
Review antihypertensive regimens at every visit, not only when out of target
Feed results back to referring GPs so shared care is aligned

pitfalls: Patients lost to follow-up after moving GP or address → confirm contact details are updated at every clinic visit
Annual review conflated with a routine transplant clinic visit without the full review content → define what the annual review must include
DNA rates not tracked → record and follow up non-attenders
Recall list not maintained centrally → assign a named administrator
pearls: Use a single database to track annual review due dates across the service
Combine the annual review with existing blood test visits to reduce patient burden
Record DNA reasons to target support at high-risk patients
Feed annual review outcomes to GPs for shared-care patients

pitfalls: No dedicated skin surveillance clinic, relying on ad hoc opportunistic checks → set up a named transplant skin surveillance clinic or pathway
Self-examination advice given once at transplant and not reinforced → repeat advice at each annual review
Patients living far from the transplant centre missing reviews → arrange shared care with local dermatology where possible
Frequency requirement not distinguished by years post-transplant → build the changing frequency into the recall system
pearls: Combine skin checks with the annual review visit to improve attendance
Give patients a self-examination guide and photograph diary
Refer early for any suspicious lesion rather than waiting for the next scheduled review
Audit alongside skin cancer incidence in the transplant cohort

pitfalls: Biopsy delayed by radiology or histopathology capacity, forcing empirical treatment → agree a rapid-access biopsy slot for suspected rejection
Reason for treating before biopsy not documented → make the reason field mandatory
Coagulopathy or single-kidney risk used inconsistently to justify treating first → agree criteria in advance with the MDT
Biopsy performed but result not available before treatment starts → track turnaround time separately
pearls: Negotiate a same-day or next-day biopsy slot with interventional radiology for suspected rejection
Fast-track histopathology reporting for transplant biopsies
Review every case where treatment preceded biopsy at the transplant MDT
Track biopsy turnaround time as a linked process measure

pitfalls: Vaccination assumed to be the GP's responsibility and not checked in clinic → make status-checking part of every autumn transplant clinic visit
No record-sharing between GP and transplant centre → ask patients to bring or confirm vaccination status
Live vaccines incorrectly given to immunosuppressed patients → ensure only inactivated influenza vaccine is used
Vaccination status not re-checked each season → build an annual reminder into the recall system
pearls: Offer on-site vaccination during the autumn transplant clinic to remove the barrier of a separate GP visit
Give patients written confirmation of vaccination for their records
Coordinate with GP practices to avoid duplicate or missed vaccination
Audit alongside pneumococcal vaccination and booster status

pitfalls: HBsAb not included in the routine annual blood panel → add it as a standing annual test
Low result identified but revaccination not actioned → build an automatic alert into the results system
Patients revaccinated elsewhere (e.g. by GP) without the result being shared → ask patients to confirm at each visit
Turnaround time for the result delays action → track result-to-action time
pearls: Bundle the HBsAb check with the existing annual review blood tests
Use an automated laboratory flag for results below 10 mIU/mL
Keep a vaccination record accessible to both transplant and primary care teams
Review results alongside other post-transplant infection surveillance data

pitfalls: 'Surgically significant' not defined locally, causing inconsistent referral → agree a local definition with the neuroscience unit before cycle 1
Discussion happens but is not documented in a retrievable place → require a coded referral log entry
Out-of-hours reporting delays discussion → audit day and night separately
Referring team unaware imaging has been reported → use an automated alert rather than relying on staff checking results
pearls: Agree the local definition of 'surgically significant' with the neuroscience unit in advance
Use a single logged referral pathway (phone plus electronic record) for every discussion
Review any delay over 1 hour at the trauma governance meeting
Keep the audit simple by using the radiology report timestamp as the start point

pitfalls: Local guideline out of date or not known to junior staff → include the transfer pathway in trauma induction
Escort training not verified before transfer → use a standard escort competency checklist
Unstable patients transferred without adequate resuscitation → reinforce the requirement to stabilise before transfer
Transfer delayed by bed availability, not process → record reasons for any delay separately
pearls: Review the transfer guideline jointly with the ambulance service and neuroscience unit annually
Use a standard transfer checklist that mirrors the NICE recommendations
Debrief any transfer that deviates from the guideline
Track transfer times alongside guideline adherence

pitfalls: Emergency admissions bypassing the standard admission checklist → build the prompt into the emergency neurosurgical admission proforma as well
Correct stocking size not available → stock a full range of sizes on the ward
Device removed for imaging/theatre and not restarted → include a restart check in the post-procedure checklist
Documentation of 'prophylaxis given' without specifying which device or when → require the specific device and start time
pearls: Make mechanical prophylaxis a same-day nursing task linked to the admission diagnosis
Audit alongside VTE risk assessment completion rates
Keep spare stockings and compression sleeves readily available on the ward
Review any gaps at the weekly ward safety huddle

pitfalls: Decision deferred repeatedly without documentation → require an explicit decision at each ward round after 24 hours
Post-operative CT not repeated to confirm no bleeding before starting LMWH → agree a standard imaging check where required locally
Different consultants applying different thresholds → agree a single departmental risk-assessment tool
LMWH started but not documented as being for VTE prophylaxis specifically → use a coded prescription indication
pearls: Build the 24-48 hour decision point into the standard post-operative ward round proforma
Agree a single risk-assessment tool across the department before cycle 1
Review any prolonged delay at the morbidity and mortality meeting
Track post-operative VTE and bleeding events as balancing measures

pitfalls: Restart decision left to the GP without a clear plan from secondary care → give an explicit restart date or review trigger on the discharge letter
No clear ownership between neurosurgery and the prescribing specialty → name the responsible team on the proforma
Decision documented but rationale not recorded → require a brief rationale field
Practice varies between consultants → agree a departmental default pathway while awaiting the full national guideline
pearls: Involve stroke medicine, cardiology or haematology early for complex anticoagulation decisions
Give a clear restart date (or review trigger) on every discharge summary
Review outcomes (rebleeding vs thromboembolism) at the morbidity and mortality meeting
Update local practice once the full multidisciplinary national guideline is published

pitfalls: EVD removal dates not consistently recorded → make removal date a mandatory nursing record field
Multiple EVDs in one patient counted inconsistently → agree that a replaced EVD counts as a new device, per the published methodology
Case definitions for infection vary between reviewers → adopt a single published case definition
Denominator data collected but not fed into a usable dashboard → assign a named person to update the dashboard monthly
pearls: Use a single infection prevention and control dashboard updated monthly
Adopt a standard published case definition for EVD-associated ventriculitis
Present rates per 1000 EVD-days alongside duration and manipulation frequency data
Compare rates over time to check the effect of any care bundle changes

pitfalls: No hand clinic capacity at weekends → agree a weekend cover arrangement or extend the 24-hour window definition consistently
Referrals miscategorised as a lower priority → use the BSSH hand injury triage app or equivalent local tool for grading
Clinic booking delays because of incomplete referral information → use a structured referral proforma
Referral time not recorded accurately → timestamp referrals electronically
pearls: Use the BSSH Hand Injury Triage guidelines/app for consistent categorisation
Protect a daily hand clinic slot specifically for green-category referrals
Review any breach of 24 hours at the weekly hand trauma meeting
Keep referral and booking data in one system to make audit straightforward

pitfalls: Hand trauma list regularly cancelled or reduced by emergency general theatre demand → secure formal protection of the list with theatre management
Delay caused by late referral from the emergency department, not theatre capacity → audit referral-to-listing time separately
Reasons for delay not recorded → make a delay-reason field mandatory
Patients unfit for surgery (e.g. intoxication, other injuries) skewing results → record and exclude these with a documented reason
pearls: Protect a specific weekly hand trauma list with agreed access rules
Track referral-to-theatre time in stages (referral to clinic, clinic to theatre) to find the real bottleneck
Review breaches monthly at the hand trauma governance meeting
Feed outcomes back to the emergency department to reinforce early referral

pitfalls: Low case numbers make month-to-month interpretation unreliable → audit over 12 months
Cubicle used for another patient at the time of a major burn admission → build an explicit escalation and de-escalation policy
Delay not recorded when the standard is not met → make the delay-reason field mandatory
Facility exists but is not thermally controlled to specification → verify against network self-assessment criteria (BBA Standards F.06.A/B)
pearls: Include the single-room requirement explicitly in the bed management escalation policy
Use the twice-daily bed utilisation data already submitted to the national Directory of Services as a data source
Review any breach at the next Burn Care Network board meeting
Align this audit with the service's biennial self-assessment against national Burn Care standards

pitfalls: Psychological input assumed to be 'not needed' by default without assessment → require an active choice rather than a blank field
Psychology team capacity insufficient to see all patients → use a tiered psychological care model with staff training for lower-tier support
Plan completed once on admission but not updated as needs change → review the psychological needs field at each MDT update
Field completed as a tick-box without genuine assessment → spot-check with patient and family feedback
pearls: Use a tiered psychological care model so ward staff can provide first-line support while specialist psychology sees the highest-need patients
Make the psychological needs field a required part of every MDT plan review, not just at admission
Involve psychology in burns MDT meetings routinely, not only on request
Track psychology referral-to-review time as a linked process measure

pitfalls: Inadequate margin identified by a non-specialist pathologist without automatic MDT flagging → use a coded histology field to trigger listing
Re-excision performed before MDT discussion out of habit → require discussion first unless there is a clinical urgency
Low case numbers → audit over 12 months
Patient not informed of the plan promptly → require a documented patient communication step
pearls: Use a coded histology margin field to enable automatic MDT list triggering
Keep a register of incomplete excisions for continuity across staff rotations
Feed outcomes back to referring dermatology/GP services
Review turnaround time from histology to MDT discussion

pitfalls: Breslow thickness not clearly stated in the histology report used for triage → require a coded thickness field from pathology
SLNB capacity/waiting times limit ability to offer it promptly → identify capacity constraints early
Patient preference not documented when SLNB is declined → require a reason field
Cases discussed at MDT before full histology is available, causing the step to be missed → build a re-check step once full histology is back
pearls: Use a coded Breslow thickness field from pathology to auto-populate the MDT list with an SLNB prompt
Give patients written information on SLNB to support shared decision-making
Audit SLNB uptake alongside re-excision rates as a package of melanoma care measures
Review any case where SLNB was omitted without documented reason at the MDT

pitfalls: Clinic-diagnosed AAA surveillance run on a separate, less robust system than the screening programme → merge onto a single recall database
Surveillance interval changed inconsistently as the aneurysm grows → automate the interval based on the latest measurement
Patients lost to follow-up after discharge from vascular clinic → use an opt-out recall system rather than relying on re-referral
Ultrasound capacity insufficient to meet 3-monthly recalls for medium AAA → identify capacity gaps before committing to the target
pearls: Use the same IT recall system as the national screening programme wherever possible
Automate interval calculation from the latest scan result
Audit alongside the screening programme's own quality assurance data
Review any patient overdue by more than 4 weeks at a monthly recall meeting

pitfalls: Referrals sent by fax or letter with no timestamp → move to a timestamped electronic referral
Severity misclassified at the point of referral → provide clear referral criteria and examples
Weekend/bank holiday referrals miscounted against working-day targets → define 'working day' clearly in the template
Triage capacity insufficient for a 1-day turnaround → identify staffing gaps before committing to the change
pearls: Use a single, mandatory electronic referral form with built-in severity flagging
Set up an automatic reminder if a referral is untriaged after 1 working day
Audit alongside the National Diabetes Foot Care Audit dataset where the unit participates
Review any breach at the weekly diabetic foot MDT

pitfalls: Referral delayed pending a formal MDT slot rather than being sent immediately → allow direct urgent referral outside the routine MDT cycle
Carotid imaging reported out of hours with no same-day action → agree an out-of-hours escalation route
Low case numbers per unit → audit over 12 months
Best medical therapy delayed while awaiting surgery → audit medical therapy start date as a secondary measure
pearls: Agree a direct, single-phone-call referral route between stroke medicine and vascular surgery
Track total time from symptom onset to surgery, not just referral to surgery
Review every case exceeding the target pathway time at the joint governance meeting
Feed outcomes into the national Sentinel Stroke National Audit Programme (SSNAP) submission

pitfalls: Rutherford classification rarely used outside vascular hubs → train spoke hospital emergency teams to classify and flag IIb cases
Patients directed to a spoke hospital first, adding avoidable transfer time → agree direct ambulance conveyance to the hub for suspected IIb ischaemia
Symptom onset time poorly documented → standardise how this is elicited and recorded
No national/local data collection system in place → set up a simple local log as an interim measure
pearls: Train ambulance and ED staff to recognise and flag suspected Rutherford IIb limb ischaemia for direct hub conveyance
Use the '6Ps' assessment consistently and document each element
Review every case exceeding six hours at the vascular morbidity and mortality meeting
Share pathway performance data across the network to drive improvement

pitfalls: Amputation booked directly by the on-call team without MDT input → build the pre-requisite field into the booking form itself
MDT discussion documented in generic terms without evidence of shared decision-making → require a specific 'patient views' field
Genuine emergencies wrongly used to bypass MDT discussion → require consultant sign-off for any emergency override
Frail or end-of-life patients not offered a broader discussion including palliative options → include amputation counsellor/palliative care input where relevant
pearls: Include the amputation counsellor and rehabilitation team in the MDT discussion, not only surgeons
Use a structured MDT proforma capturing revascularisation options considered and patient preference
Review every emergency-override case at the vascular governance meeting
Track amputation counselling and rehabilitation referral rates as linked outcomes

pitfalls: Course stopped early at discharge because the discharge prescription is overlooked → build the remaining LMWH days into the discharge prescription automatically
Bleeding risk assessment not documented, making it unclear whether the recommendation applies → make risk assessment a mandatory pre-op step
Mechanical prophylaxis omitted on the amputated/residual limb without considering the contralateral leg → clarify in the order set that intermittent pneumatic compression is used on the remaining leg
Early discharge to rehabilitation interrupting the course → communicate the remaining course clearly in the transfer letter
pearls: Build the full 7-day course, including any discharge supply, into a single order set
Communicate VTE prophylaxis plans clearly in transfer letters to rehabilitation units
Audit alongside post-amputation VTE and bleeding event rates as balancing measures
Review any early discontinuation at the vascular governance meeting

pitfalls: Referral may happen by phone/bleep with no written record: agree with the crisis team in advance that every referral is also logged electronically
Patients who abscond before triage or assessment are not comparable: exclude them explicitly and report the number excluded
Staff may push back that 'we always refer everyone': collect a baseline before assuming this, since local card CR-3174/3392 show gaps even where staff believe compliance is high
A single term for the crisis service may not match every trust's naming: agree the exact service name with the ED and CAMHS leads before data collection starts
Out-of-hours attendances may use a different on-call pathway: capture time of day so out-of-hours performance can be reported separately
pearls: Recruit an ED consultant and a CAMHS/crisis team consultant as joint audit leads so the fix can be built into both systems
Agree before cycle 1 exactly what counts as 'referral made' (a bleep call, an electronic referral, or both)
Use the ED's existing self-harm coding list to identify the sample quickly rather than manually screening all attendances
Present the baseline to both teams together so the fix is owned jointly, not seen as an ED-only or CAMHS-only problem
Hand the audit and the mandatory-field build to the incoming CAMHS liaison trainee at rotation, with the re-audit date fixed in the departmental audit calendar

pitfalls: Repeat attenders may be seen by different professionals each time, fragmenting the record: search by patient identifier across all attendances, not by single episode
'Suitably skilled mental health professional' is not defined locally: agree a short list of qualifying roles with CAMHS before data collection
Attendances that end in the young person leaving before assessment will look like a 'fail' for reasons outside the team's control: record and report separately
Staff may see repeat self-harm as 'attention seeking' and be less thorough: present the data without individual blame and focus on the system flag
Six months may be too short to find repeat attenders in a small unit: extend the window rather than lowering the sample size
pearls: Ask the ED data team to run the repeat-attendance search electronically rather than manually cross-referencing notes
Recruit the CAMHS lead nurse to help define 'suitably skilled' before cycle 1 so there is no dispute at analysis
Share the individual (anonymised) attendance timelines with the team, not just the percentage, as this is the most persuasive way to show gaps
Agree with IT in advance whether the repeat-attendance flag can be built as an automatic alert, since this is what worked in comparable services
Keep the audit with the liaison team rather than a rotating CAMHS trainee, since continuity of care is the point being measured

pitfalls: A generic 'risk management plan' may be wrongly counted as a safety plan: define the required elements (triggers, coping strategies, contacts) in the data collection tool
Assessments completed out of hours by a duty worker may use a paper safety plan that is not scanned into the electronic record: check both paper and electronic sources
Families may decline to be involved: record this as a valid reason rather than a failure of the young person's own agreement
Clinicians may feel a template is too rigid for individual presentations: pilot the template with two or three clinicians and gather feedback before full rollout
Improvement may fade once the pilot team's enthusiasm wears off: build the template into the mandatory record rather than relying on a reminder poster
pearls: Base the template on an existing published safety-planning tool (e.g. a suicide safety plan format) rather than designing one from scratch
Involve a young person or family representative in reviewing the template wording before rollout
Agree with reception/admin that the safety plan can be printed on the spot so families leave with a physical copy
Present both the completion rate and a couple of anonymised examples of good versus poor plans to help clinicians see what 'good' looks like
Hand ownership of the re-audit to the CAMHS or crisis team's own quality improvement lead rather than a single trainee, since teams rotate

pitfalls: Height and weight recorded at a GP or school nurse visit outside the ADHD clinic may be missed: agree a single source of truth for measurements before starting
A telephone or video review cannot include physical measurements: record whether the appointment was face-to-face and exclude remote reviews from the numerator
The interval differs by age band (under 10 vs over 10): pre-sort the sample by age so the correct schedule is applied to each patient
Teaching alone rarely moves this measure, as the library shows an electronic record change is needed to convert centiles automatically
Non-attendance at review appointments will look like a monitoring gap: record DNAs separately from measurements not taken at an attended appointment
pearls: Recruit the ADHD clinic administrator to help build the automatic reminder, since they control the appointment system
Agree the exact NICE interval definitions with the clinic team before data collection to avoid disputes at analysis
Use the growth chart itself (not just a text entry) as the source of truth, since a plotted point is easy to verify
Share the topic card's finding that a dedicated clinic model (not teaching) achieved the biggest gains, to set expectations for the fix
Timetable the re-audit for after the reminder system has been running for a full monitoring cycle (6 months), not sooner

pitfalls: Recording a raw heart rate/BP without comparing to the age-normal range should not count as a pass: define 'compared' as an explicit centile or normal/abnormal statement in the data tool
Dose changes made by a shared-care GP may not be visible to the specialist service: include a data-sharing check with primary care before starting
The library shows posters and teaching failed here because the electronic system could not calculate centiles: budget for an IT change, not just an education session
Patients who decline monitoring should be recorded as a specific category, not counted as a system failure
Multiple small dose titrations in a short period could be double-counted: use the most recent dose change in the audit period as the index event
pearls: Involve the electronic prescribing/IT team from the outset, since the library shows a system fix (not teaching) is what worked elsewhere
Use an age-appropriate blood pressure centile calculator built into or linked from the record, rather than a paper chart
Present the topic card evidence (teaching failed, system change worked) to secure sign-off for an IT change request
Pilot the mandatory link with one prescriber before rolling out trust-wide, to catch workflow problems early
Fix the re-audit date at 6 months so at least one full monitoring cycle has passed since the change

pitfalls: If BP centiles are rarely calculated in the first place (as the library shows), the true denominator of 'confirmed high BP' may be undercounted: report the number of patients with any BP centile recorded alongside the audit result
A single high reading without repeat measurement should not count towards the denominator: require a second confirmatory reading before counting a case
Referral pathways to paediatric hypertension services vary between trusts: confirm the correct local referral route before data collection
Cases may be too few for a stable percentage: report as a proportion with the raw numerator and denominator, not just a percentage
Prescribers may continue medication while awaiting referral without recording a reason: capture this explicitly rather than assuming an oversight
pearls: Work with the ADHD clinic's admin team to search the record for any BP centile entries above the 95th centile, since these cases are rare and easy to miss manually
Agree the referral pathway and target response time with paediatric cardiology/hypertension before cycle 1
Because numbers will be small, present individual case summaries (anonymised) alongside the percentage to make the point clearly
Build the alert as a hard stop or strong prompt in the electronic record, since a soft reminder is unlikely to succeed given how rarely centiles are used
Keep this audit running continuously (rather than a single cycle) since new high-BP cases will appear slowly over time

pitfalls: A generic 'review in clinic' note without a specific date or trigger should not count as a pass: define this precisely in the data tool
New starters may be prescribed by an out-of-area or private provider whose notes are not available: exclude and record these separately
Staff may see stopping plans as unrealistic for long-standing behaviour: present the audit as measuring documentation of intent, not a requirement to actually stop
The library shows side-effect discussion fell after criteria changed between cycles in one service [3416]: keep the same criteria across both cycles
Family or paid carers may not be present at review to discuss stopping: record whether they were consulted, as this affects the quality of the plan
pearls: Base the mandatory field on the exact NG11 1.8.5 wording so there is no ambiguity about what counts as a strategy
Recruit the learning disability pharmacist to help design and monitor the field, since they typically run the STOMP register
Share the topic card's consultant advice (count actual dose reductions, not just plans) directly with the team to set the improvement target
Time the re-audit to align with the annual STOMP reporting cycle already required by NHS England, so data collection is not duplicated
Keep the audit register with the learning disability team pharmacist rather than a rotating psychiatry trainee, for continuity

pitfalls: 'No clear response' may be under-recorded because staff default to continuing rather than actively reassessing: define the audit to flag any review note lacking an explicit response statement as a fail
Environmental or psychological interventions may be tried without being recorded as linked to the medication review: cross-check care plans as well as prescription notes
Carers and care home staff may resist stopping medication they believe is working: record any documented carer view as part of the justification, not as an automatic pass
A change of prescriber partway through the period could mean the 6-week review was never formally handed over: check for a gap in responsibility
Numbers may be small in a single team: consider a longer collection window or pooling across neighbouring learning disability teams
pearls: Use the exact NG11 wording ('no indication of a response at 6 weeks') as the pass/fail definition to avoid subjective judgement calls
Involve a learning disability nurse or support worker who knows the person well in the review, since they can describe real behavioural change
Present the finding alongside the topic card's headline gap (50.6% with no clear indication [3584]) to show this is a known, high-harm, fixable problem
Agree the pharmacy hard-stop build with IT and pharmacy governance before cycle 1 so the change can go live immediately after presentation
Track actual dose reductions and stops at re-audit, not just documentation, as this is what the topic card identifies as missing from every existing audit

pitfalls: Annual health checks are often nurse-led using a template that may not prompt for mental health explicitly: check the template itself as well as individual entries
A tick-box 'mental health: normal' with no detail may be too weak to count as a real review: agree with the primary care team what counts as adequate detail before data collection
People who decline or do not attend are excluded from this audit but should be tracked separately, since non-attendance is itself a known access problem
GP data systems vary (EMIS, SystmOne): the exact template location for annual health checks will differ between practices
A learning disability nurse or GP may feel this adds to an already long consultation: build the change into the existing template rather than adding a separate step
pearls: Work with the practice's learning disability register lead, who already runs the annual health check DES, to make this change with minimal extra burden
Use a short, validated question (for example, a simple mood and behaviour change screen) rather than a lengthy new tool
Present the audit to the primary care network learning disability lead, since a template change there can spread across several practices at once
Agree in advance how referral for a mental health concern found at the check will be actioned (to the community learning disability team), so the change closes a real loop
Fix the re-audit to the next annual health check cycle so the same patients can be tracked over time

pitfalls: A generic community mental health team may see the person without recognising the learning disability, especially if mild: check the referral coding as well as the outcome
Rural or smaller services may have no dedicated learning disability specialist and rely on liaison input: define what counts as adequate liaison before data collection
Referral letters may not state the person has a learning disability if it is not the presenting reason: cross-check against the GP learning disability register
Waiting times to a specialist team may be longer than to a generic team, creating pressure to bypass the specialist route: record time to assessment for both
Historic referrals may predate a service reorganisation: use only referrals from the last 12 months to reflect current pathways
pearls: Cross-reference the referral list against the GP learning disability register to make sure no relevant referral is missed
Agree a single definition of 'learning disability expertise' with both teams before starting, to avoid disputes over borderline cases
Recruit a joint audit lead from both the learning disability and generic mental health teams so the fix is owned by both
Use the audit findings to support a business case for a formal liaison arrangement if none currently exists
Keep the referral log query script so the re-audit can be run quickly by whoever holds the audit next

pitfalls: A team may be named as 'key worker' rather than an individual, which does not meet the intent of the standard: define 'named' as a specific person in the data tool
Key workers may change with staff turnover without the care plan being updated: check the last care plan review date alongside the named worker
People open to both a community learning disability team and a separate community mental health team may have two different named workers, causing confusion: record and flag this as a fail
Caseload lists may be out of date: verify the current caseload with the team manager before sampling
Care plans stored only on paper in some services will need manual review alongside the electronic record
pearls: Agree the definition of 'serious mental illness' (psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe depression) with the team before sampling to keep the population consistent
Ask the team manager for an up-to-date caseload list rather than relying on a historic report
Present the audit alongside the QS142 statement wording so the standard is unambiguous to the team
Build the key worker field into whatever care planning software is already in use, rather than a separate document
Repeat the audit after the next round of staff changes, since key worker continuity is most at risk during turnover

pitfalls: A brief 'continue as before' note should not count as a pass: define the required content (specific clinical reason) in the data tool
Patients seen only by a GP on a shared-care basis may not have specialist review documented at all: check both specialist and GP records
Long-stay patients with decades of unchanged prescribing may have no recent documented rationale anywhere: report this finding directly rather than assuming it exists
Staff may resist a formal reminder as bureaucratic if they know the patient well: frame the change as a safeguard against unexamined long-term prescribing, per LeDeR-type learning
A dose reduction attempted and reversed due to relapse should still count as active review, not treated the same as no review at all
pearls: Use the STOMP register (already required by NHS England) as the sampling frame so the audit does not duplicate existing data collection
Recruit the learning disability pharmacist to lead the annual reminder build and review the findings
Present the QS142 statement 5 wording directly to prescribers so the annual documentation requirement is unambiguous
Track whether annual review leads to any actual dose changes over time, not just documentation, to show real impact
Align the re-audit date with the trust's existing annual STOMP reporting deadline to avoid duplicate data pulls

pitfalls: Women may already be stable on valproate after multiple failed alternatives, making a switch clinically inappropriate: record this as a documented, reasoned decision rather than a fail
Perinatal and adult mental health teams may hold separate valproate registers: reconcile both before sampling to avoid double counting or missed cases
Small numbers are likely given how few women of childbearing potential remain on valproate once the pregnancy prevention programme is enforced: report raw numbers alongside any percentage
A woman may not disclose she is sexually active or planning pregnancy, affecting the urgency of the discussion: record what was asked, not assumed
Switching medication carries its own relapse risk: frame the change as ensuring the discussion happens, not mandating a switch
pearls: Use the mental health pharmacist-held valproate register as the single source of truth for the sampling frame
Involve both perinatal and adult mental health pharmacy leads, since patients often move between these services
Present the topic card's consultant advice directly to the team to justify why this specific angle (switching, not just ARAF completion) is the audit focus
Agree with the team in advance what counts as an acceptable 'alternatives ineffective or not tolerated' justification
Keep the valproate register under pharmacy ownership so the re-audit can be run without waiting for a trainee rotation

pitfalls: Pregnancy planning may be discussed informally in a routine appointment without a specific documented field: agree with clinicians to actively ask and record this at every relevant review
Women may not disclose pregnancy plans to a mental health worker they see infrequently: report the number of women asked as well as the number referred
Specialist perinatal services may have geographic or capacity limits, making referral to a generic secondary service the only option: record this as a partial pass with the reason given
Retrospective identification of 'planning a pregnancy' entries may be difficult if not coded: consider prospective data collection over a fixed window instead of retrospective search
The record may show a referral made but never actioned by the receiving service: check the perinatal team's own referral log for confirmation, not just the sending note
pearls: Recruit the perinatal mental health service lead as a joint audit lead with the adult community mental health team
Use a structured yes/no prompt rather than free text so future searches are reliable
Agree a simple referral pathway and response time standard with the perinatal service before starting, so the change has somewhere to route referrals
Present the finding to the trust's perinatal mental health network (many now exist under the NHS Long Term Plan), which can support scaling the change
Keep prospective data collection running via the new prompt so the re-audit is a simple data pull rather than a fresh manual search

pitfalls: Postpartum psychosis is rare, so numbers will be very small: report raw numerators/denominators and consider a rolling collection over 12-24 months rather than a single 3-month window
Out-of-hours referrals may go through a different crisis pathway with less clear time-stamping: check both in-hours and out-of-hours logs

A woman may present to a general adult crisis team unfamiliar with the postpartum psychosis red flags and be triaged as routine: check for missed or delayed recognition, not just delay after correct triage
Referral and assessment times may be recorded inconsistently (referral received vs. referral accepted): agree a single time-stamp definition before starting
A perinatal mental health service may not operate 24/7 in smaller areas, meaning the target route is unavailable out of hours: record and report this system gap
pearls: Work with the crisis team and perinatal mental health service together, since the referral usually crosses between them
Use the rarity of the condition as an argument for prospective, continuous data collection via the new flag, rather than a fixed 3-month audit window
Base the change on a simple, recognisable red-flag checklist for postpartum psychosis so referrers do not need specialist perinatal knowledge
Present any near-miss or delayed case (even outside the identified events) as a case study to strengthen the argument for the timer system
Escalate any finding that the specialist perinatal service is unavailable out-of-hours to commissioners, as this is a systemic, not just documentation, gap

pitfalls: A discussion may happen verbally without being recorded: agree with the team that this is a documentation standard, and undocumented discussions still count as a fail
Specialist perinatal pharmacy advice (e.g. from UKTIS or a specialist pharmacist) may be sought but not linked in the main note: check pharmacy correspondence as well as the clinical note
Women who are not breastfeeding and have no plans to should be excluded, but this needs to be explicitly documented, not assumed
The discussion needs to be specific to the medication prescribed, not a generic breastfeeding leaflet: define this distinction in the data tool
Views may change over the postnatal period (a woman may start breastfeeding after initially not planning to): capture the date of the woman's current status alongside the discussion date
pearls: Recruit the perinatal mental health pharmacist to help build and monitor the mandatory field
Use an established resource (such as a specialist medicines-in-pregnancy/breastfeeding information service) as the reference point for what a 'complete' discussion covers
Present the change as reducing legal and clinical risk from undocumented advice, which helps secure clinical engagement
Time the re-audit for 6 months to capture a full cohort of women moving through pregnancy to the postnatal period
Keep a simple log of specialist pharmacy queries made, as this is a useful secondary marker that the discussion is happening

pitfalls: Nursing reviews may be recorded in general nursing notes rather than a dedicated seclusion record, making them hard to find: search both sources
The 'independence' requirement may be poorly understood by staff: provide clear guidance on what counts as involvement in the original decision
Overnight and asleep-patient reviews may follow a modified schedule under local policy: record these separately rather than counting them as missed reviews
A template alone gave only modest gains in one service (75% to 83%) with minimal further change on a statistical process control chart [3552]: plan for ongoing monitoring, not a single fix
Staff may see 2-hourly review as excessive during long seclusion episodes: reinforce the safeguarding rationale in training, not just the form
pearls: Base the proforma directly on Mental Health Act Code of Practice paragraph 26.134 wording so staff can see exactly what is required
Use a physical or electronic timer/alert to prompt the 2-hourly review, since the library shows structural prompts outperform teaching alone
Recruit a senior ward nurse as the audit lead, since they can identify realistic barriers to documenting independence
Present the topic card's finding that huddles and weekly meetings raised consultant review compliance from under 70% to over 90% [3105], to support a similar nursing huddle model
Track average seclusion duration alongside review compliance, since the library shows a huddle model also reduced average seclusion time from 30 to 20 hours [3105]

pitfalls: Long or intermittent seclusion episodes reaching the 12-hour-in-48-hours trigger may be harder to track than continuous episodes: build a running total into the seclusion record, not a manual calculation
'Independent' membership may be compromised if the same small on-call team covers both the original decision and the review: record and flag this explicitly
IMHA involvement may not be arranged in time, especially out of hours: track whether the patient has an IMHA and whether they were invited
Numbers will be small: consider extending data collection to 6-12 months and pooling with other wards in the same secure service if needed
A review that happens late may still be recorded as 'done' without the delay being visible: always capture the time from trigger to review, not just yes/no
pearls: Build the 8-hour/12-hour trigger calculation into the seclusion record software so staff do not need to calculate it manually
Involve the trust's Mental Health Act administrator, who is well placed to track prolonged seclusion episodes across wards
Use this audit to also check IMHA involvement, since the two safeguards are meant to work together
Present near-miss cases (episodes close to but not reaching the trigger) to show the alert would have helped, even with a small confirmed sample
Since this trigger is rare, keep it as a standing, continuously monitored indicator rather than a one-off audit

pitfalls: Staff may complete a generic care plan template not specific to seclusion, missing the required elements: check against the exact four headings, not a general impression of completeness
Bedding/clothing and dietary needs may be managed verbally by nursing staff without being written into the plan: this should still count as a fail, since the standard requires documentation
Care plans may be updated as seclusion continues, so audit the most recent version, but also check the plan was in place from early in the episode, not only by the time it ended
A well-intentioned but generic 'as per care plan' note without specific content should not count as a pass
Fatigue during very long seclusion episodes may mean updates lapse over time: sample from both early and later points in longer episodes if resources allow
pearls: Base the structured proforma exactly on Code of Practice paragraph 26.147 so nothing required is left to interpretation
Recruit ward matrons/senior nurses to pilot the new proforma before a full rollout, since they complete these plans in practice
Link this audit with the seclusion review audits (nursing/medical/independent) so a single data collection exercise can gather several linked measures
Share examples of complete versus incomplete plans anonymised from the audit findings, to help staff see what 'good' looks like
Keep the proforma under the ward's own clinical documentation folder so it survives staff rotation

pitfalls: A generic ward risk assessment done on admission may be wrongly counted as the leave-specific risk assessment: require it to be dated at or after the leave decision and to reference the leave itself
Escorted vs unescorted leave carry different risk profiles: record which type of leave was granted, since a blanket risk assessment may not address both
For patients on long-term leave with periodic short extensions, distinguish the first grant (audited here) from routine extensions
Forensic/secure wards may already do this well due to existing MDT risk review processes: report results by ward type to identify where the gap is greatest
A documented risk assessment that is a copy-paste from a previous one without genuine reassessment should not count as a pass
pearls: Use the existing library audit [3245] baseline (83% missing) as the starting comparison point to show the scale of the problem
Recruit the Mental Health Act administrator, who processes every section 17 form, to help identify the sample and enforce the mandatory field
